parts.note: Men Only was a British men's magazine; the forerunner of such a read is pictured as a little book for chaps, the cheap pamphlet sold by pedlars

explanation.surface: A question about what came before a well-known men's magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: Men Only was a British magazine for men. Split the answer as CHAP + BOOK and it is a 'book for chaps', and the chapbooks of pedlars were the popular reading of earlier centuries.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheap popular pamphlets hawked by pedlars were the mass reading matter that came before modern magazines.

parts.note: the shop saying holds that the buyer is always right; the clue leaves out the buyer

explanation.surface: A riddle about who is never wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The retail motto 'the — is always right' is quoted with its subject missing.
explanation.definitionFit: A shopper or client is the person who, by the retail motto, can never be wrong.

clue.text: Have a party with your share, love

parts.note: a do is a party
a ration is one's allotted share

explanation.surface: An invitation to celebrate with your portion of affection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Have' and 'with' only link the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep devotion or worship is a form of love.

parts.note: defensive players in football share a name with the college lawns along the river Cam at Cambridge

explanation.surface: A question about football players beside Cambridge's river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Backs are the college grounds along the river Cam in Cambridge; backs are also defenders in football.
explanation.definitionFit: Defenders in football bear the same name as the riverside college lawns in Cambridge.

parts.note: open means frank or candid
an air is a look or manner

explanation.surface: A candid person seems healthy and invigorated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so' links; 'fresh' is the outdoor sense, as in an outdoor concert.
explanation.definitionFit: Happening outdoors is out in fresh conditions, the sense of an outdoor event.

clue.text: A liquid from a bottle gets you high

parts.note: perfume poured from a bottle is scent

explanation.surface: A drink poured from a bottle makes you tipsy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'liquid from a bottle' and 'high' suggest drink, but the liquid is perfume and the height is a climb.
explanation.definitionFit: A climb upwards is what carries a walker to a high point.

clue.text: Is a tensor used by bearers of this?

definitions.text: Is a tensor used by bearers of this?

parts.words: Is a tensor used by bearers of this?
parts.note: a tensor is something that stretches, and bearers carry a litter for the wounded with the same name

explanation.surface: A question whether stretcher-bearers use some technical device.
explanation.walkthrough: Tensor comes from Latin for stretch, so a tensor is a thing that stretches; the bearers carry the litter called by that name.
explanation.definitionFit: A litter carried by bearers shares its name with anything that stretches, as a tensor does.

clue.text: Oddly enough that is the Roman law for state enemies

indicators.note: oddly says the pieces are put in an odd, rearranged order

parts.note: ie is the abbreviation for id est, that is
lex is the Latin word for law

explanation.surface: A curious remark about how ancient Rome treated public enemies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly enough' rearranges IE and LEX.
explanation.definitionFit: Banishment from one's country was the punishment for enemies of the state.

definitions.meaning: deals with, as one deals with a patient or problem
outings or meals paid for by someone else

explanation.surface: Someone manages complimentary amusements.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is a verb (deals with), the other a plural noun (things paid for by someone else).
explanation.definitionFit: To deal with something, and things given as a gift, both fit the same word.

clue.text: Dish to display cook's art? Hardly

definitions.text: Dish to display cook's art? Hardly

parts.words: Dish to display cook's art? Hardly
parts.note: the thin prison gruel looks like ...-... but needs hardly any skill

explanation.surface: A doubt whether a certain dish shows off culinary talent.
explanation.walkthrough: Skilly is thin gruel served in workhouses and prisons; its name looks like 'skill' plus y, yet it needs no cooking skill.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin watery oatmeal broth served in workhouses is a dish that shows off no culinary art.

parts.note: a spot is a dotted fabric pattern
a check is a squared fabric pattern

explanation.surface: Someone inspects a couple of fabric designs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two textile patterns' supplies both pieces: spot and check.
explanation.definitionFit: A random inspection made without warning is a kind of examination.

parts.note: the poet Longfellow wrote of the great German waterway lined with castles, and a 'long fellow' of a river suits it too

explanation.surface: A reference to a river with castles in a Longfellow poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The castle-lined river of Germany appears in Longfellow's 'The Golden Legend'; it is also a long river, a 'long fellow'.
explanation.definitionFit: The great German waterway is famous for the castles along its gorge, celebrated by Romantic poets.

clue.text: They're pretty stony with no chums

parts.note: O is nought, nothing, so it stands for no
pals are chums

explanation.surface: People so hard-hearted that they have no friends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stony' pretends to mean unfriendly, and 'pretty stony' a person; the definition is gems, pretty stones.
explanation.definitionFit: Iridescent gemstones are attractive stones, hence pretty and stony.

clue.text: Much intended, we hear, in the share-out

indicators.note: says the phrase is spoken and the matching sound written down

parts.note: much is 'a lot' and intended is 'meant', together a lot meant

explanation.surface: A lot was meant to go into the division of goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' turns 'a lot meant' into the word of the same sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A portion given out in a distribution is one's share, and the distributing is a share-out.

definitions.meaning: one who instructs and improves the mind morally
the Latin root aedificare means to build, so the word literally means a builder

explanation.surface: A self-help guru who builds up one's confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: To edify is to improve someone morally; the word comes from Latin for building, so a builder is the literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: One who instructs uplifts the mind, and by etymology is a builder of edifices.

parts.note: economists' term for income from services such as shipping and insurance, as opposed to visible trade in goods

explanation.surface: A complaint about pay that never reaches the earner.
explanation.walkthrough: Invisible earnings are national income from services rather than goods; the clue reads it as money nobody sees.
explanation.definitionFit: Trade income from services is called by the word for unseen, contrasting with goods.

parts.note: Jonathan Swift's brutish human creatures in Gulliver's Travels, a name later used for any louts

explanation.surface: Thugs who move quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swift' looks like 'fast', but it is Jonathan Swift, whose Gulliver's Travels has the brutish human beasts whose name became a word for louts.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's brutes in Gulliver's Travels gave English a name for coarse, rowdy people.

clue.text: Where the policeman should know the time

definitions.text: Where the policeman should know the time

parts.words: Where the policeman should know the time
parts.note: a constable walks a patrol route, and a musician keeps time by following the rhythm

explanation.surface: A remark that officers on patrol ought to know what time it is.
explanation.walkthrough: A constable patrols his round, and in music to be in time is to keep to the rhythm.
explanation.definitionFit: Patrolling a route is the constable's duty, and in music keeping time means following the pulse.

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of the words could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Something was got round by digging with spades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges BY SPADES.
explanation.definitionFit: Going round an obstacle instead of through it is to avoid it.

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of the next word might be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A question whether hypocritical talk might cheer someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges LIVENS.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypocritical whining talk is cant, and to whine tearfully is the same sense.

clue.text: This butter-dish for the Upper House

definitions.meaning: in Judges, Jael brought forth butter in a ... dish, the Bible's phrase
befitting the House of Lords, Britain's upper chamber of Parliament

explanation.surface: A dish of butter destined for Parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: Judges 5:25 says Jael 'brought forth butter in a lordly dish'; the House of Lords is the upper house of the UK Parliament.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand and noble, fitting for peers, as in the Bible's grand dish for butter.

parts.note: the poet's sister and companion shares her name with a drawstring handbag

explanation.surface: A poet's friend in loose clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: William Wordsworth's sister was his constant companion; 'baggy' points to the drawstring handbag of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet's sister kept the Grasmere journals and walked beside him, and her name also labels a drawstring handbag.

parts.note: to chew over a question is to talk it through

explanation.surface: Thinking a problem over carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: To chew over a question is to debate it.
explanation.definitionFit: Talking a matter over in conversation is to debate it.

parts.note: a frame of sliding beads used for counting; the 'please' asks for the frame to be passed

explanation.surface: A request at a shop counter for beads.
explanation.walkthrough: The bead frame is a counting device; 'counter' looks like a shop counter.
explanation.definitionFit: A counting frame of beads on wires is used for arithmetic.

clue.text: Arm bands? Why not, if they've joined up?

definitions.text: Arm bands? Why not, if they've joined up?

parts.words: Arm bands? Why not, if they've joined up?
parts.note: sleeve badges worn by soldiers, and with brass bands of the army in mind the joined-up word reads as brass plus arms

explanation.surface: Musings on whether military bands of recruits might be called arm bands.
explanation.walkthrough: Brassards are armbands worn on the sleeve; the clue plays on brass bands, which, once their players have joined up, might be called arm bands.
explanation.definitionFit: A badge or band worn round the upper sleeve is the meaning of the French-derived word.

clue.text: Picked men, but fellow-players aren't supposed to hear

definitions.meaning: a team chosen to play, as a side picked for a match
a remark on stage spoken to the audience that the other actors pretend not to hear

explanation.surface: Selected men with a secret their team-mates mustn't overhear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fellow-players' suggests team-mates, but these are actors on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: A chosen team is a side, and an actor's remark to the audience is unheard by others on stage.

clue.text: Are not (Sandy appropriately asks) the combatants here?

parts.note: na is the Scots word for not

explanation.surface: A Scotsman asks whether the fighters are present.
explanation.walkthrough: Sandy is a stock name for a Scot, which is why the Scots 'na' for 'not' is appropriate.
explanation.definitionFit: The enclosed space where gladiators fought is where the combatants are.

clue.text: As the Roman said with such frequency

definitions.text: As the Roman said with such frequency

parts.words: As the Roman said with such frequency
parts.note: Latin for 'I hear', and the range of frequencies the ear can hear

explanation.surface: Something a Roman said often.
explanation.walkthrough: In Latin the word means 'I hear'; audio frequency is the range the ear can hear. 'frequency' pretends to mean 'often'.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for I hear, and the frequency band within human hearing.

clue.text: "O world! O life! O time! On whose last steps I —" (Shelley)

definitions.text: "O world! O life! O time! On whose last steps I —" (Shelley)

parts.words: "O world! O life! O time! On whose last steps I —" (Shelley)
parts.note: the missing last word of the opening line of Shelley's poem A Lament, the verb for going up steps

explanation.surface: Fill in the gap in a line of Shelley.
explanation.walkthrough: The line opens Shelley's 'A Lament'; one ascends steps, so the missing verb is the word for going up.
explanation.definitionFit: Going up steps is to ascend them, the verb the poet uses for life's last stairs.

parts.note: lawn is fine linen, so a linen frock is a lawn dress, which said quickly is the washerwoman's title

explanation.surface: What a washerwoman wears.
explanation.walkthrough: Lawn is a fine linen, so a 'lawn dress' sounds like the word for a washerwoman.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who washes clothes for a living is the definition of the word.

parts.note: Sue is a girl's name
Des is a boy's name, short for Desmond

explanation.surface: Children described as a girl and a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kids' looks like children, but kid is soft goatskin leather, as is suede.
explanation.definitionFit: Kid leather and napped leather are both soft materials for gloves, so the plurals pair up.

definitions.meaning: mixed sweets sold as a selection of different kinds

explanation.surface: Secret documents compared to a tin of sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classified' suggests secret, but it means sorted; a box of mixed toffees is a selection of varieties.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorted into groups, and a mixture of various kinds, as in a box of sweets.
